study.title: Emergency help and political solidarity
study.research_question: How do tenants distinguish emergency help from political solidarity?
study.unit_of_analysis: A sequenced interview excerpt from one tenant
study.provenance: Instructor-authored synthetic course material. No real people were interviewed and no named model generated these records.
study.corpus_limit: The eight excerpts support classroom comparison only. They provide no evidence about a real neighborhood or population.

excerpts.context: The interviewer has asked how the tenant first encountered the mutual-aid network.
excerpts.text: When the rent went up, the grocery deliveries got us through the last week of the month. At that point I did not know who organized them.

excerpts.context: Later in the same interview, the tenant describes what changed after several months of childcare exchanges.
excerpts.text: After a few months of taking turns with childcare, I started going to the tenants' meetings. The first time I spoke was about the broken elevator.

excerpts.context: The interviewer asks whether receiving emergency rent support changed the tenant's involvement.
excerpts.text: I was grateful for the emergency fund, but I kept it separate from politics. I did not attend meetings and I still do not think of myself as an organizer.

excerpts.context: The tenant explains why participation ended after initially helping with deliveries.
excerpts.text: Once the delivery rota became a requirement, it stopped feeling like help. I missed two shifts, people kept messaging me, and I left the group.

excerpts.context: The interviewer asks how relationships formed through repair exchanges affected later action.
excerpts.text: Fixing things together meant we already trusted one another when the eviction notices arrived. Six of us wrote the petition and delivered it together.

excerpts.context: The tenant responds to the interviewer's use of the word solidarity.
excerpts.text: The organizers call it solidarity. For me it was mostly a way to make it to payday. That does not mean I wanted a political identity attached to it.

excerpts.interviewer_provenance: Instructor-authored simulation of a bounded AI interviewer; no live model was used
excerpts.context: The initial answer was: 'I delivered groceries twice.' The generated follow-up asked: 'Did those deliveries change how you understood your relationship with other tenants?'
excerpts.text: I learned people's names and felt less alone in the building. I would not say it made me political, but I was more willing to ask what others needed.

excerpts.context: The interviewer asks why the tenant continued attending meetings after no longer needing material support.
excerpts.text: The food deliveries ended for me, but by then the meetings were where we compared what the landlord had told each floor. I stayed because acting separately was not working.

candidate_model_proposal.candidate_theme: Mutual aid transforms practical dependence into political solidarity.
candidate_model_proposal.access_route: cached synthetic record; no API call

revised_claim_record.candidate_theme: In several interviews, repeated mutual-aid exchanges created opportunities for political identification, but practical reliance did not consistently become political solidarity and could also generate withdrawal when help was experienced as obligation.
revised_claim_record.context_note: Movement from help to collective action appears in several accounts, but other tenants separate assistance from politics or withdraw when reciprocity becomes obligation.
revised_claim_record.alternative_interpretation: Mutual aid creates opportunities for political identification without reliably producing it.
revised_claim_record.researcher_decision: Narrow the model proposal and retain practical coping and obligation as competing interpretations.
revised_claim_record.access_route: cached synthetic record; no API call
revised_claim_record.researcher_memo: The strong conversion language initially directed attention toward T01 and T04. Reading T02, T03, T05, and T06 together made that account look too linear.
